question: What are we doing?
v_answer: Meeting the patient, making 100% sure we have the right person, checking allergies, and opening their hospital record.

question: Why are we doing it?
v_answer: Wrong-patient errors (wrong blood sample, wrong medicine, wrong operation) are some of the most serious mistakes in hospitals. An allergy that isn't recorded can kill when a medicine is given. Everything later depends on this step CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED .

question: What does the trainee actually do?
v_answer: 1. Introduce yourself: name and role ("Hello, I'm Dr Ruhan, one of the surgical doctors"). 2. Ask the patient to SAY their full name and date of birth. Never read it to them ("You're Ayesha Khan, right?") — anxious people say yes to anything. 3. Compare their answer with the wristband AND the notes. At least two identifiers must match CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (locally usually name + date of birth + hospital/MR number CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION ). 4. Ask: "Do you have any allergies? What happened when you had it?" Check the allergy band (often red CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION ). 5. Ask: "Can you tell me what operation you're here for / what's brought you in?" 6. S1: check a responsible adult can take them home and stay for 24 hours (needed for day surgery) CLINICAL INTERPRETATION . 7. Record arrival time; open the admission record.

question: What are we doing?
v_answer: A structured conversation to learn what's wrong, what other illnesses and medicines the patient has, and anything that makes surgery unsafe.

question: Why are we doing it?
v_answer: Most of the information needed for a diagnosis comes from the history. Many dangers (blood thinners, recent food, pregnancy) are invisible unless you ask CLINICAL INTERPRETATION .

question: What does the trainee actually do?
v_answer: 1. Main complaint: "What's the problem? Where's the pain? When did it start? Does it move? What makes it worse? 0–10?" 2. Red-flag questions (warning signs). S1: fever? yellow skin/eyes? dark urine/pale stools? constant pain over 24 h? pain through to back? S2: pain moved from belly button? vomiting? appetite? fever? urine symptoms? diarrhoea? women: last period, chance of pregnancy, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain; men: testicle pain. 3. Other illnesses: heart, lungs, blood pressure, diabetes, kidney, liver, bleeding problems, previous clots, sleep apnoea, thalassaemia/sickle cell. 4. Medicines: everything, especially blood thinners (and when last taken), diabetes medicines, GLP-1 injections, steroids, BP tablets, the pill, herbal remedies. 5. Allergies: what and what happened. 6. Previous anaesthetics: any problems; family members with serious anaesthetic problems. 7. Social: smoking, alcohol, drugs, who's at home. 8. Last food and drink: exact time and what. 9. Pregnancy (whenever pregnancy is possible for this patient): asked privately and sensitively; test offered with consent if there is any doubt CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (NICE NG45). 10. Summarise back and ask "Anything else you want to tell me?"

question: What does the trainee actually do?
v_answer: 1. Attach the oxygen finger clip; read oxygen % and heart rate; look at the wave. 2. Put on the BP cuff; wait for the reading. 3. Count breaths for 30–60 seconds. 4. Measure temperature. 5. Check alertness (ACVPU). 6. Ask pain score 0–10. 7. Feel the pulse — regular or irregular? 8. Weight/height if not recorded; finger-prick sugar if diabetic. 9. Calculate NEWS2 and pick the right response. 10. Repeat any odd reading.
